blocks.content: kubectl get lists objects of a given type, the single most frequently typed kubectl command, and the natural starting point for almost any interaction with a cluster.

kubectl get pods, kubectl get deployments, kubectl get services, the same command, applied to whatever object type you actually want to see, listing every matching object in the current namespace by default.

blocks.alt: The starting point for interacting with almost anything in a cluster

blocks.content:
kubectl get pods
kubectl get deployments
kubectl get services

code.content:
kubectl get pods
kubectl get deployments
kubectl get services

codes.bash:
kubectl get pods
kubectl get deployments
kubectl get services

blocks.content: -o wide adds extra columns to the normal table view, -o yaml or -o json dumps the object's full, raw definition, useful when you need to see (or script against) the complete underlying data, not just a summary.

blocks.alt: From a quick summary table to the full, raw object definition

blocks.content: By default, get only shows objects in your current namespace, -A (or --all-namespaces) removes that boundary, showing everything across the entire cluster in one view.

blocks.alt: Removing the namespace boundary, for a cluster-wide view

blocks.content: -w keeps the command running, streaming updates as objects change, useful for watching a rollout progress or a new Pod come up in real time, instead of repeatedly re-running the plain command.

blocks.alt: A live, continuously updating view instead of a single static snapshot

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: kubectl get lists objects of any type, and is the natural starting point for almost any interaction with a cluster.
-o for output format, -A for every namespace, and -w to watch live are the flags worth knowing by heart.
